doctrine:
**Forum shopping** is the repetitive availment of several judicial remedies in different courts, simultaneously or successively, all substantially founded on the same transactions and the same essential facts and circumstances, and all raising substantially the same issues either pending in or already resolved adversely by some other court. The ultimate test is the vexation caused to the courts and the parties by asking different fora to rule on the same or related causes or to grant the same or substantially the same reliefs, creating the possibility of conflicting decisions (reiterated).

**A lawyer who, while a certiorari petition against an execution order is pending, files a second certiorari petition against a later execution order in the same case, seeking the same reliefs, commits forum shopping, even though the two petitions assail different orders and the client disclosed the first petition in the verification and certification.** The lawyer violates **Canon II, Section 23** of the CPRA (forum shopping), Canon I, Section 1, **Canon III, Sections 2 and 7** (prohibition against frivolous suits and abuse of court processes, including unduly impeding the execution of a warranted judgment), and the Revised Lawyer's Oath.

Willful and deliberate forum shopping is a **serious offense** under Canon VI, Section 33(n) of the CPRA, punishable under Section 37(a) by disbarment, suspension from the practice of law for more than six months, and/or a fine exceeding PHP 100,000.00. Under **Section 39**, when there are aggravating circumstances and no mitigating circumstances, the Court may impose suspension or a fine of up to double the maximum prescribed. A prior administrative sanction and lack of remorse were treated as two aggravating circumstances, and the Court imposed a one-year suspension instead of the three months recommended by the IBP Board of Governors.
facts:
Complainant Carolina Bautista-Pangilinan, through her attorney-in-fact Miriam Bustamante, won an ejectment case before the MeTC of Quezon City, Branch 35, against Vivian Sanchez, who was assisted by respondent Atty. Engracio M. Icasiano. The property was covered by TCT No. 125621 in complainant's name. The MeTC Decision of May 8, 2013 ordered Sanchez to vacate, and a writ of execution was issued on November 21, 2013 under an Omnibus Order of the same date.

On February 14, 2014, through Atty. Icasiano, Sanchez filed a petition for certiorari and prohibition (First Petition) in the RTC, raffled to Branch 84. After Atty. Icasiano moved for the judge's inhibition, it was re-raffled to Branch 93, which dismissed it in a Decision dated July 15, 2015. Meanwhile, on January 28, 2015, complainant moved to implement the writ of execution, which the MeTC granted on May 5, 2015. On July 13, 2015, while the First Petition was still pending, Atty. Icasiano filed for Sanchez a petition for certiorari, prohibition and mandamus (Second Petition) assailing the May 5, 2015 Order. It was raffled to Branch 88 and, after the judge inhibited, re-raffled to Branch 105, which dismissed it on November 17, 2016 and declared the petitioners guilty of forum shopping. That Decision was not appealed.

Complainant filed a disbarment complaint charging Atty. Icasiano with forum shopping and land grabbing. He answered that the MeTC Decision was void because Bustamante's special power of attorney was invalid, that Bustamante also lacked authority to file the disbarment complaint, and that there was no forum shopping because the two petitions assailed different orders and he had even asked that the Second Petition be assigned to Branch 93.

The IBP Investigating Commissioner recommended dismissal, finding the land-grabbing charge unsupported, noting the absence of an SPA for the disbarment complaint, and finding no forum shopping because the MeTC Decision was void. The IBP Board of Governors (Resolution No. CBD-XXV-2022-04-24, April 23, 2022) reversed and recommended suspension for three months, finding that both petitions assailed the grant of execution, that the Second Petition was filed while the First was pending, and that the RTC's unappealed finding of forum shopping stood.
issues: Whether Atty. Icasiano committed forum shopping and violated the CPRA and the Lawyer's Oath by filing the two certiorari petitions.
What penalty should be imposed on him.
ruling:
**1. Yes.** The Court agreed with the IBP Board of Governors. It was undisputed that Atty. Icasiano filed two separate but similar certiorari petitions against two orders of the MeTC, the November 21, 2013 Omnibus Order and the May 5, 2015 Order, both of which granted complainant's motions for execution. **"Although respondent questioned two separate orders and his client disclosed the filing of the First Petition in her Verification and Certification,"** he sought the same reliefs in the Second Petition: (1) to maintain the status quo of his client's possession of the property; (2) to prohibit the implementation of the writs of execution; and (3) to declare that the MeTC judge acted with grave abuse of discretion in granting the motions for execution. He was therefore guilty of forum shopping. RTC Branch 105 had also found forum shopping in its unappealed November 17, 2016 Decision, and that finding stands.

His conduct violated Canon II, Section 23 of the CPRA, under which a lawyer "shall not knowingly engage or through gross negligence in forum shopping" and "shall not institute or advise the client to institute multiple cases to gain leverage in a case, to harass a party, to delay the proceedings, or to increase the cost of litigation." It also violated Canon I, Section 1 (efficient and effective delivery of justice); Canon III, Section 2 (duty to promote respect for laws and legal processes and assist in the speedy and efficient administration of justice) and Section 7 (a lawyer shall not unduly impede the execution of a warranted judgment or abuse court processes); and the Revised Lawyer's Oath.

**2. Suspension from the practice of law for one year.** Willful and deliberate forum shopping is a serious offense under Canon VI, Section 33(n), punishable by disbarment, suspension exceeding six months, and/or a fine exceeding PHP 100,000.00 (Section 37[a]). Atty. Icasiano had previously been reprimanded with a stern warning in *Quilendrino v. Atty. Icasiano* (A.C. No. 9332, February 27, 2019) for violating Canon 8, Rule 8.01 and Canon 11, Rule 11.03 of the Code of Professional Responsibility, and he showed no remorse, insisting that he did not commit forum shopping. **With two aggravating and no mitigating circumstances, Section 39 allowed the Court to impose a suspension of up to double the maximum prescribed**, and it found a one-year suspension appropriate, rather than the three months recommended by the IBP.
disposition: Atty. Engracio M. Icasiano was found GUILTY of violating Canon II, Section 23; Canon I, Section 1; Canon III, Sections 2 and 7 of the CPRA; and the Revised Lawyer's Oath. He was SUSPENDED from the practice of law for one year, effective immediately upon receipt of the Decision, with a STERN WARNING that a repetition will be dealt with more severely. He was directed to file a manifestation that his suspension has started, copy furnished all courts and quasi-judicial bodies where he has appeared as counsel. Copies were ordered furnished the Office of the Bar Confidant, the Office of the Court Administrator, and the IBP.

bar_questions.q: Atty. Reyes represents Lina, who lost an ejectment case. When the MeTC granted the plaintiff's motion for execution, Atty. Reyes filed for Lina a petition for certiorari and prohibition with the RTC, asking that Lina's possession be maintained, that the writ of execution be enjoined, and that the MeTC judge be declared to have acted with grave abuse of discretion. While that petition was pending, the MeTC issued a second order directing implementation of the writ. Atty. Reyes then filed a second petition for certiorari, prohibition and mandamus with another RTC branch against the second order, seeking the same three reliefs. Lina disclosed the first petition in her verification and certification. Charged administratively, Atty. Reyes argues that there is no forum shopping because the two petitions assail different orders and the first petition was disclosed. Is Atty. Reyes administratively liable?

alac.answer: Yes. Atty. Reyes committed forum shopping and is administratively liable under the CPRA.
alac.legal_basis: Forum shopping is the repetitive availment of several judicial remedies in different courts, simultaneously or successively, all substantially founded on the same transactions and essential facts, and raising substantially the same issues; the ultimate test is the vexation caused by asking different fora to grant the same or substantially the same reliefs, with the possibility of conflicting decisions. Under Canon II, Section 23 of the CPRA, a lawyer shall not knowingly or through gross negligence engage in forum shopping. Canon III, Section 7 prohibits a lawyer from unduly impeding the execution of a warranted judgment and from abusing court processes. Questioning two separate orders and disclosing the first petition do not negate forum shopping where the same reliefs are sought. (Bautista-Pangilinan v. Atty. Icasiano, A.C. No. 13752, August 6, 2025)
alac.application: Both petitions arise from the same ejectment judgment and attack the same thing: the execution of that judgment. Both seek the same reliefs, namely to keep Lina in possession, to stop the writ, and to declare the MeTC judge guilty of grave abuse. The second was filed while the first was pending in another branch, creating the risk of conflicting rulings. That the second petition targets a later implementing order, and that the first petition was disclosed, does not change the identity of the reliefs. Filing it also unduly impeded the execution of a final ejectment judgment.
alac.conclusion: Atty. Reyes is liable for forum shopping and abuse of court processes under Canon II, Section 23 and Canon III, Section 7 of the CPRA.

bar_questions.q: In an administrative case, Atty. Cruz was found to have committed willful and deliberate forum shopping. The records show that he had previously been reprimanded with a stern warning by the Supreme Court for another violation, and throughout the proceedings he insisted that he did nothing wrong. No mitigating circumstance was shown. The IBP Board of Governors recommended suspension from the practice of law for three months. Is the recommended penalty proper?

alac.answer: No. Three months is too light; the Court may suspend him for more than six months, and up to double the maximum prescribed, as in Icasiano, where it imposed a one-year suspension.
alac.legal_basis: Willful and deliberate forum shopping is a serious offense under Canon VI, Section 33(n) of the CPRA, punishable under Section 37(a) by disbarment, suspension from the practice of law for a period exceeding six months, and/or a fine exceeding PHP 100,000.00. Under Section 39, if one or more aggravating circumstances and no mitigating circumstances are present, the Court may impose suspension or a fine not exceeding double the maximum prescribed, and may in its discretion impose disbarment. A prior administrative sanction and lack of remorse were treated as two aggravating circumstances. (Bautista-Pangilinan v. Atty. Icasiano, A.C. No. 13752, August 6, 2025)
alac.application: Since Atty. Cruz committed a serious offense, the minimum suspension is more than six months, so three months is below the prescribed range. His previous reprimand and his lack of remorse are aggravating circumstances, and no mitigating circumstance offsets them, so Section 39 allows the Court to go up to double the maximum. In Icasiano, on the same combination of circumstances, the Court rejected the IBP's three-month recommendation and imposed a one-year suspension with a stern warning.
alac.conclusion: The IBP's three-month recommendation is improper; a suspension exceeding six months, such as one year, is warranted.

bar_questions.q: In the same situation as Atty. Reyes in the first question, the second RTC branch found that Lina and her counsel committed forum shopping. (a) What is the effect of willful and deliberate forum shopping on the second petition? (b) Lina argues that because she truthfully disclosed the first petition in her certification against forum shopping, she complied with the Rules and cannot be guilty of forum shopping. Is she correct?

alac.answer: (a) It is a ground for summary dismissal of the second petition with prejudice, and it also constitutes direct contempt and a cause for administrative sanctions. (b) No. Disclosure in the certification does not cure forum shopping.
alac.legal_basis: Under Rule 7, Section 5 of the Rules of Court, if the acts of the party or counsel clearly constitute willful and deliberate forum shopping, this is a ground for summary dismissal with prejudice and constitutes direct contempt, as well as a cause for administrative sanctions. Forum shopping is determined by whether the party seeks the same or substantially the same reliefs from different fora on the same facts, creating the possibility of conflicting decisions; in Bautista-Pangilinan v. Atty. Icasiano (A.C. No. 13752, August 6, 2025), the Court held that counsel committed forum shopping although the client "disclosed the filing of the First Petition in her Verification and Certification," because the same reliefs were sought.
alac.application: (a) Filing a second petition seeking the same reliefs while the first is pending is willful and deliberate forum shopping, so the second petition may be summarily dismissed with prejudice, and Lina and her counsel are exposed to contempt and, for counsel, disciplinary sanctions. (b) The certification requirement is a separate duty to inform the court; truthful disclosure avoids a false certification but does not make it proper to ask two courts for the same reliefs at the same time. The vexation and risk of conflicting rulings remain.
alac.conclusion: The second petition is dismissible with prejudice, and Lina's disclosure of the first petition does not excuse the forum shopping.

notes: The ejectment case number appears in the record as Civil Case No. 10-39977, 35-09-39977 and 35-39977. The Court agreed with the IBP Board of Governors except as to the penalty, and did not separately rule on respondent's defenses that the MeTC Decision was void and that Bustamante lacked an SPA, or on the land-grabbing charge (found unsupported by the Investigating Commissioner). The Court described willful and deliberate forum shopping as the serious offense under Section 33(n) without separately discussing intent. Rule 7, Section 5 in Bar question 3 is basic procedural law not discussed in the Decision. Only three Justices took part (Zalameda and Marquez, JJ. were on official business).
